dialogue.english: Okay, take the first street on the right.

dialogue.speaker: رَاكِب
dialogue.english: Here, and keep the change.

dialogue.speaker: سَوَّاق
dialogue.english: Thank you, have a good day.

response.english: Okay, but the road is crowded right now.

pair.english: Can you take me to the hospital?

pair.english: How much is the fare to Jowban?

response.english: Twenty riyals and that's it.

lessons.culture: In Jeddah, Makkah and Madinah, taxis are the main way to get around in the city. Meters are standard, and you can hail taxis on the street or call for one. Most drivers know the major landmarks well, so it helps to name a neighborhood or famous building rather than a street address.

exercises.prompt: The driver asks: "وَيْن تَبِي تَرُوح؟" (Where do you want to go?) Tell him you want to go to the Grand Mosque.

too_formal.feedback: Correct in written Arabic, but far too formal for speaking to a taxi driver.

exercises.tip: "أَبِي" plus a verb is how Hejazi speakers say what they want to do.

exercises.prompt: The driver hands you change and says: "تَفَضَّلْ، الْبَاقِي." (Here, the change.) Thank him in the Hejazi way.

too_formal.feedback: Too formal; in Hejazi the standard response to a small favor or tip is a blessing.

exercises.tip: "اللَّهُ يُعْطِيكَ الصِّحَّة" is the everyday Hejazi way to say thank you for a favor.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "شَغِّلْ _____ لَوْ سَمَحْتَ." English: Turn on the meter please.

too_formal.feedback: That describes the device; "الْعَدَّاد" (the meter) is the everyday word.

exercises.tip: "الْعَدَّاد" literally means 'the counter' and is the word for a taxi meter.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "_____ هِيهِ، هَذَا الْبَيْت." English: Stop here, this is the building.

too_formal.feedback: Fine in writing, but the spoken command "قِفْ" is what you actually say to a driver.

exercises.tip: A short, direct command like "قِفْ" is normal with a taxi driver.

exercises.prompt: Translate into Hejazi Arabic: "I want to go to the airport."

too_formal.feedback: Grammatically correct, but this is written-style Arabic, not how people speak.

exercises.tip: In Hejazi, "أَبِي" plus a verb is the natural way to express what you want to do.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Keep the change."

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but too formal for handing a driver a tip.

exercises.tip: "الْبَاقِي لَك" (the rest is for you) is the simple, everyday way to say keep the change.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means "How much is the fare to here?"

too_formal.feedback: Grammatically correct, but far more formal than everyday speech.

exercises.tip: "بِكَمْ" is how you ask 'how much' in Hejazi; "لِهِيهِ" means 'to here.'

exercises.prompt: Which is the Hejazi way to tell someone to keep to the right?

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but too formal; Hejazi speakers use the simpler verb "خَلِّيكَ."

exercises.tip: "خَلِّيكَ" means 'stay' or 'keep'; it is the everyday way to give directions.

exercises.prompt: Put these in the right order: "لَوْ سَمَحْتَ / الْعَدَّاد / شَغِّلْ"

too_formal.feedback: Fine in formal writing, but spoken Arabic puts the verb first, then the object, then the politeness word.

exercises.tip: In spoken Hejazi: verb first, then object, then "لَوْ سَمَحْتَ" at the end.

exercises.prompt: Put these in the right order: "الْآن / هِيهِ / قِفْ"

exercises.tip: A direct command like "قِفْ هِيهِ" (stop here) is how you actually speak to a driver.

reply.english: Straight ahead, you'll find it on your right.

dialogue.speaker: سَائِل
dialogue.english: Excuse me, where is the hospital?

dialogue.speaker: مُسَاعِد
dialogue.arabic: دُغْرِي مِنْ هِيهِ، وَتِلَقَّاهُ عَلَى شِمَالَك.
dialogue.transliteration: dughri min hiih, wa tilaqahu 3ala shimaalak.
dialogue.english: Straight ahead from here, you'll find it on your left.

dialogue.speaker: سَائِل
dialogue.english: Is it very far?

dialogue.speaker: مُسَاعِد
dialogue.english: No, about ten minutes.

dialogue.speaker: سَائِل
dialogue.english: Okay, thanks.

dialogue.speaker: مُسَاعِد
dialogue.arabic: عَلَى الْرَّحْبِ وَالسَّعَة، خَبِّرْنِي إِذَا احْتَجْتَ شَيْء.
dialogue.transliteration: 3ala ar-rahb wa as-sa3a, khabirni idha ihtajt shay.
dialogue.english: You're welcome, let me know if you need anything.

dialogue.speaker: سَائِل
dialogue.english: I want to go to the bank. From where?

dialogue.speaker: مُسَاعِد
dialogue.arabic: اِرْجِعْ شُوَيّة وَلِفّ يَمِين. الْبَنْك بِشَارِعِ الإِمَام.
dialogue.transliteration: irji3 shuwayya wa liff yameen. al-bank bi-shaari3 al-imam.
dialogue.english: Go back a bit and turn right. The bank is on Imam Street.

dialogue.speaker: سَائِل
dialogue.english: Is it far?

dialogue.speaker: مُسَاعِد
dialogue.arabic: لاَ، قَرِيب جِدًّا. سَاعَة عَلَى الرِّجْلَيْن.
dialogue.english: No, very close. A moment's walk.

pair.english: Where is the public park?

response.arabic: دُغْرِي مِنْ هِيهِ، حَوَالَي عِشْرْ دَقَايِق.
response.english: Straight ahead from here, about ten minutes.

pair.english: I want to go to the school. Where is it?

response.arabic: لِفّ يَمِين هِيهِ، وَالْمَدْرَسَة عَلَى الزَّاوِيَة.
response.english: Turn right here, the school is on the corner.

pair.english: Is the street closed?

response.arabic: إِي، لاَزِم تِرْجِعْ شُوَيّة وَتِلِفّ بِطَرِيق ثَانِيَة.
response.transliteration: i, lazim tirja3 shuwayya wa tiliff bi-tareeg thaniya.
response.english: Yes, you have to go back a bit and take another route.

pair.english: How many minutes to the airport?

response.english: If you hurry, about half an hour.

lessons.culture: In Jeddah, Makkah and Madinah, most neighborhoods are built around narrow streets and alleys. People often give directions using landmarks like mosques, shops, or squares rather than street names. It is common for locals to be very helpful with lost travelers, especially near the holy sites.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks: "وَيْنَ تَبِي تَرُوح؟" (Where do you want to go?) Tell them you want to go to the mosque.

too_formal.feedback: Too formal for everyday conversation.

exercises.tip: "أَبِي" is the Hejazi way to say what you want.

exercises.prompt: Someone gives you directions and you want to thank them. What do you say?

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but too formal; a simple thanks is more natural.

exercises.tip: "شُكْرًا كِتِير" (thanks a lot) is the everyday way to say thanks.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "لَوْ سَمَحْتَ، _____ الصَّيْدَلِيَّة؟" English: Excuse me, where is the pharmacy?

too_formal.feedback: That is the formal/written way to ask 'where'; Hejazi speakers say "وَيْنَ."

exercises.tip: "وَيْنَ" is how you ask 'where' in Hejazi.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "اِمْشِ دُغْرِي _____ السُّوق." English: Walk straight until the end of the market.

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning; "لِآخِرِ" (to the end) is the everyday way to say it.

exercises.tip: "لِآخِرِ" means 'to the end' and is commonly used in directions.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Is it far from here?"

too_formal.feedback: Grammatically correct, but too formal for everyday questions.

exercises.tip: "بَعِيد؟" (Is it far?) is the simplest way to ask about distance.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I'm lost, can you help me?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but far too formal; Hejazi is more direct.

exercises.tip: "تَايِه" means 'lost'; "فيك" is a casual, friendly way to ask if someone can help.

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but the spoken verb "لِفّ" is much more natural.

exercises.tip: "لِفّ" means 'turn'; "يَمِين" means 'right'; "شِمَال" means 'left.'

exercises.prompt: Which is the Hejazi way to say "Straight ahead"?

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but "دُغْرِي" is the everyday Hejazi word.

exercises.tip: "دُغْرِي" is the common Hejazi word for 'straight ahead.'

exercises.prompt: Put in order: "الإِشَارَة / عِنْدَ / يَمِين / لِفّ"

too_formal.feedback: Fine in writing, but "لِفّ" is the spoken way.

exercises.tip: Verb first ("لِفّ"), then direction, then location.

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning; the Hejazi version is simpler.

exercises.tip: Question word first, then the thing being asked about, then the detail.

phrases.english: Do you stop at the Riyadh roundabout?

dialogue.speaker: رَاكِب
dialogue.english: Where is the bus stop for the university?

dialogue.speaker: مُوَظَّف
dialogue.arabic: دُغْرِي مِنْ هِيهِ حَوَالَي مِائَة مِتْر.
dialogue.transliteration: dughri min hiih hawala mi2a mitr.
dialogue.english: Straight ahead from here, about a hundred meters.

dialogue.speaker: مُوَظَّف
dialogue.english: Just two riyals.

dialogue.speaker: رَاكِب
dialogue.english: This bus goes to the university, not the airport?

dialogue.speaker: مُوَظَّف
dialogue.arabic: إِي، الْبَاص رَقَمْ ثَلاَثَة يِرُوح الْجَامِعَة. الْأَحْمَر يِرُوح الْمَطَار.
dialogue.transliteration: i, al-bass raqam talata yirooh al-jami3a. al-ahmar yirooh al-mataar.
dialogue.english: Yes, bus number three goes to the university. The red one goes to the airport.

dialogue.speaker: رَاكِب
dialogue.english: Okay. How many hours to get there?

dialogue.speaker: مُوَظَّف
dialogue.arabic: حَوَالَي نِص سَاعَة إِذَا مَا فيهْ زِحْمَة.
dialogue.transliteration: hawala niss sa3a idha ma feeh zihma.
dialogue.english: About half an hour if there's no traffic.

pair.english: Does this bus go to the airport?

response.english: No, you need number five.

pair.english: Is there an empty seat?

response.english: Yes, here on your right.

pair.english: Please, let me off at the mosque.

response.english: Sure, I'll call you when we get there.

pair.english: The bus is crowded, should I wait for the next one?

response.english: The next one is a bit emptier. Wait.

lessons.culture: Buses in Hejazi cities like Jeddah are the main form of public transport. Small minibuses (microbuses) operate specific routes and are faster for short trips. Long-distance buses connect Jeddah to Makkah and Madinah. The buses run frequently, especially during daylight hours, and are quite affordable.

exercises.prompt: The driver asks: "وَيْنَ تَبِي تَنْزِل؟" (Where do you want to get off?) Tell him you want to get off at the mosque.

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but too formal; Hejazi uses "أَبِي" for what you want.

exercises.tip: "أَبِي" plus a verb is how you say what you want in Hejazi.

exercises.prompt: The bus driver says: "تَفَضَّلْ، الْبَاقِي." (Here, the change.) Thank him naturally.

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but overly formal for a bus transaction.

exercises.tip: A simple blessing or "شُكْرًا" is the Hejazi way to say thanks.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "وَيْنَ _____ الْبَاص؟" English: Where is the bus stop?

too_formal.feedback: That is plural; for a single stop use "مَحَطَّة."

exercises.tip: "مَحَطَّة" means a station or stop.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "هَالْبَاص _____ الْجَامِعَة؟" English: Does this bus go to the university?

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but "يَرُوح" is more natural in spoken Hejazi.

exercises.tip: "يَرُوح" (he goes / it goes) is the common Hejazi verb for going.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "The bus is very crowded."

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but "زِحْمَة" is the everyday Hejazi word for crowded.

exercises.tip: "زِحْمَة" (crowded, congested) is used for buses, roads, or any crowded place.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Please let me off here."

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but the Hejazi version with "نَزِّلْنِي" is more natural.

exercises.tip: "نَزِّلْنِي" means 'let me down'; it is the verb used for getting off a bus.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means "How much is the ticket?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning; "بِكَمْ" is more direct and everyday.

exercises.tip: "بِكَمْ" is how you ask the price of something in Hejazi.

exercises.prompt: Which is the natural way to say "There's an empty seat"?

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but too formal; Hejazi uses the simpler "فيهْ."

exercises.tip: "فيهْ" means 'there is'; it is much more common than the formal يُوجَد.

exercises.prompt: Put in order: "الْجَامِعَة / لِلْ / يَرُوح / هَالْبَاص"

too_formal.feedback: Fine in writing; the spoken version is simpler.

exercises.tip: In Hejazi, the subject comes first, then the verb, then the destination.

exercises.prompt: Put in order: "جِدًّا / زِحْمَة / الْبَاص"

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning; "زِحْمَة" is more casual and everyday.

exercises.tip: Subject first, then "زِحْمَة," then intensity word like "جِدًّا."

dialogue.speaker: سَائِح
dialogue.english: Excuse me, where is the Sacred Mosque?

dialogue.speaker: مَحَلِّي
dialogue.arabic: دُغْرِي مِنْ هِيهِ. مَا فيهْ وَاحِد بِهِدِ الْمَدِينَة مَا يَعْرِفْ الْمَسْجِد!
dialogue.transliteration: dughri min hiih. ma feeh wahid bi-hadh al-madeena ma ya3rif al-masjid!
dialogue.english: Straight ahead from here. There's not a single person in this city who doesn't know the Mosque!

dialogue.speaker: سَائِح
dialogue.english: I want to go to a restaurant for a bit.

dialogue.speaker: مَحَلِّي
dialogue.arabic: فيهْ مَطْعَم حِلْو بِشَارِعِ الإِمَام. يِعْطُونَ أَكْلَة هَيَّاجَة!
dialogue.transliteration: feeh mat3am hilw bi-shaari3 al-imam. yi3toon akla hayyaja!
dialogue.english: There's a nice restaurant on Imam Street. They make amazing food!

dialogue.speaker: سَائِح
dialogue.english: Is it far?

dialogue.speaker: مَحَلِّي
dialogue.arabic: لاَ يَا غَالِي، حَوَالَي سَاعَة عَلَى الرِّجْلَيْن.
dialogue.transliteration: la ya ghali, hawala sa3a 3ala ar-rijlayn.
dialogue.english: No my friend, about a twenty-minute walk.

dialogue.speaker: سَائِح
dialogue.english: Okay. Thanks a lot.

dialogue.speaker: مَحَلِّي
dialogue.arabic: أَهْلاً وَسَهْلاً يَا أَخِي. اِسْتَمْتِع بِالتُّرَاثْ!
dialogue.transliteration: ahlan wa sahlan ya akh. istamti3 bi-at-turath!
dialogue.english: You're welcome my brother. Enjoy the heritage!

pair.english: Where is the nearest pharmacy?

response.arabic: فيهْ وَحِدَة بِشَارِعِ الْعَابِدِين قَرِيب جِدًّا.
response.transliteration: feeh wahda bi-shaari3 al-3abideen gareeb jiddan.
response.english: There's one on Abideen Street very close.

pair.english: Is there a school nearby?

response.arabic: إِي، هِيهِ عَلَى الزَّاوِيَة بِشَارِع الْمَلِكْ.
response.english: Yes, it's on the corner of King Street.

pair.english: I want to go to the hospital. Where is it?

response.english: The main hospital is near the Sacred Mosque.

pair.english: Is there a bank close by?

response.arabic: إِي، بَنْك الرِّيَاض عَلَى طُول الشَّارِع.
response.english: Yes, Riyadh Bank is right down the street.

lessons.culture: Jeddah has both old and new neighborhoods with modern facilities mixed in with traditional markets. The main shopping district near the Red Sea corniche has restaurants, banks, and shops. Makkah and Madinah are spiritual centers with the Sacred Mosque (Masjid al-Haram) in Makkah and the Prophet's Mosque (Masjid an-Nabawi) in Madinah being the most important landmarks.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks: "وَيْنَ تَبِي تَرُوح؟" (Where do you want to go?) Tell them you want to go to the bank.

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but too formal for everyday speech.

exercises.tip: "أَبِي" is the natural Hejazi way to say what you want.

exercises.prompt: A local asks: "شُو إِسْمُ الْمَدْرَسَة الْقَرِيبَة؟" (What is the name of the nearby school?) Tell him it is Al-Noor School.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but "اسْمُهَا" is more natural in spoken Hejazi.

exercises.tip: "اسْمُهَا" (its name) is the simple Hejazi way to identify something.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "وَيْنَ أَقْرِبْ _____ مِنْ هِيهِ؟" English: Where is the nearest hospital from here?

too_formal.feedback: That is an adjective; the noun "مُسْتَشْفَى" (hospital) is what you need.

exercises.tip: "مُسْتَشْفَى" is the word for hospital.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "فيهْ مَطْعَم حِلْو _____ الْمِنْطَقَة؟" English: Is there a nice restaurant in the area?

too_formal.feedback: That is too formal; "فِي" is the everyday word.

exercises.tip: "فِي" means 'in' and is used for locations.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Where is the nearest bank from here?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning; Hejazi uses "وَيْنَ" and "هِيهِ" which are more casual.

exercises.tip: "أَقْرِبْ" means 'nearest'; "مِنْ" means 'from.'

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Is there a good restaurant in the area?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but far too formal; Hejazi uses "فيهْ" casually.

exercises.tip: "حِلْو" literally means 'sweet' but is used for 'good' or 'nice' in everyday speech.

exercises.prompt: Which word means 'the Sacred Mosque'?

too_formal.feedback: While respectful, "الْمَسْجِد الْحَرَام" is the standard name.

exercises.tip: "الْحَرَام" means 'the Sacred' or 'the Forbidden'; "الْمَسْجِد" means 'the mosque.'

exercises.prompt: Which is the word for 'school' in Hejazi?

too_formal.feedback: That means 'university', not school.

exercises.tip: "مَدْرَسَة" is the word for school; "جَامِعَة" is university.

exercises.prompt: Put in order: "الْمُسْتَشْفَى / وَيْنَ / أَقْرِبْ"

too_formal.feedback: Fine in formal Arabic; the Hejazi word is "وَيْنَ."

exercises.tip: Question word first, then the adjective "أَقْرِبْ," then the noun.

exercises.prompt: Put in order: "الْمِنْطَقَة / فِي / حِلْو / مَطْعَم / فيهْ"

too_formal.item: يُوجَدُ مَطْعَمٌ جَيِّدٌ فِي هَذِهِ الْمِنْطَقَةِ
too_formal.feedback: Grammatically correct, but Hejazi uses "فيهْ" casually.

exercises.tip: "فيهْ" (there is) comes first; then noun, adjective, location phrase.

dialogue.speaker: أبو أحمد
dialogue.english: Yes, get in.

dialogue.speaker: محمد
dialogue.arabic: الله يُعَافِيكْ، أَبِي أَرُوحْ الْبَلَدْ الْقَدِيمْ
dialogue.transliteration: allah yu3aafik, abi aroo7 il-balad il-gadeem
dialogue.english: God keep you well, I want to go to the Old City.

dialogue.speaker: أبو أحمد
dialogue.arabic: عِشْرِين دَقِيقَة تَقْرِيبًا، إِنْ شَاءَ الله
dialogue.english: About twenty minutes, God willing.

dialogue.speaker: أبو أحمد
dialogue.english: By the meter.

dialogue.speaker: محمد
dialogue.english: Okay, stop here, please.

dialogue.speaker: أبو أحمد
dialogue.english: Is here good?

dialogue.speaker: محمد
dialogue.english: Yes, good, thank you.

dialogue.speaker: أبو أحمد
dialogue.english: God protect you, goodbye.

pair.english: Are you free?

response.english: Yes, get in.

pair.english: How much is the fare?

response.english: By the meter.

pair.english: I want to go to the Old City.

response.english: At your service.

pair.english: How long does the way take?

response.english: About twenty minutes.

pair.english: Will you drop me at the station?

response.english: Yes, right away.

lessons.culture: Taxis are the primary way to get around in Jeddah and the cities of Makkah and Madinah. Drivers usually respond to requests with "حَاضِرْ" (at your service), and you can thank them with "الله يُعَافِيكْ" (God keep you well) or "شُكْرًا" (thank you). Saying where you want to go directly, and then "وَقِّفْ هِنِّ" to stop at your destination, is the normal way to ride.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I want to go to the Old City."

too_formal.feedback: This is formal written Arabic; everyday Hejazi speech uses "أَبِي أَرُوحْ...".

exercises.tip: "أَبِي أَرُوحْ" is the everyday pattern for "I want to go".

exercises.prompt: Which word means "taxi"?

too_formal.feedback: This is the fuller formal term for taxi; everyday speech just says "تَاكْسِي".

exercises.tip: "تَاكْسِي" and "بَاصْ" are both everyday loanwords.

exercises.prompt: A taxi driver asks "وَيْنَ تَبِي؟" (Where do you want to go?). Say: to the station.

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic rather than the everyday spoken answer.

exercises.tip: "لِـ" plus the place ("لِلْمَحَطَّة") is the short way to say "to the station".

exercises.prompt: Complete: "كَمْ _____ الطَّرِيق؟" Meaning: How long does the way take?

too_formal.feedback: This is a formal full question; the spoken version is much shorter.

exercises.tip: "تَاخِذْ" is the everyday spoken form of "it takes".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Stop here, please." (to a man)

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic; the everyday imperative is "وَقِّفْ".

exercises.tip: "هِنِّ" is the Hejazi "here", and "لُو سَمَحْتْ" makes it polite.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "الأجرة؟ / بكم"

too_formal.feedback: This is a formal, wordier version of the same question.

exercises.tip: "بِكَمْ" comes first in this everyday question.

exercises.prompt: Which word is a driver's polite reply meaning "at your service"?

too_formal.feedback: This is a more elaborate, formal-sounding version of the same courtesy.

exercises.tip: "حَاضِرْ" means "ready, at your service" and is a very Hejazi reply.

exercises.prompt: You ask a driver "فاضي؟" and he is not free. What does he say?

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic; the everyday one-word answer is "مَشْغُول".

exercises.tip: "فَاضِي" is free, "مَشْغُول" is busy.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "What time does the bus come tomorrow?"

too_formal.item: فِي أَيِّ سَاعَةٍ يَصِلُ الْبَاصُ غَدًا؟
too_formal.feedback: This is a formal written question; everyday speech uses "بُكْرَا" and "يِجِي".

exercises.tip: "بُكْرَا" (or "بُكْرَة") is "tomorrow"; "يِجِي" is the everyday form of "comes".

exercises.prompt: Complete: "ابي اروح البلد _____." Meaning: I want to go to the Old City.

too_formal.feedback: This is a more literary word for "old"; everyday Hejazi speech says "الْقَدِيم".

exercises.tip: "الْقَدِيم" is the word for old; in Hejazi "ق" is often pronounced like "g".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Bus."

too_formal.feedback: This is the standard written word for bus; spoken Hejazi Arabic uses the loanword "بَاصْ".

exercises.tip: "تَاكْسِي" and "بَاصْ" are both borrowed words.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Will you drop me at the station?" (to a man)

too_formal.item: هَلْ تَسْتَطِيعُ أَنْ تُوَصِّلَنِي إِلَى الْمَحَطَّة؟
too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic; the everyday question is just "تُوصِلُّنِي...؟".

exercises.tip: Say the verb with a rising voice; no extra question word is needed.

challenge.title: أَنْتَ سَائِح فِي الْحِجَاز
challenge.instructions: You are a tourist in Hejazi-speaking area. Have a short conversation with a local about getting around the city. Use phrases from the unit to ask for directions, find a place to eat, and get advice about visiting important sites. Write your own replies in the conversation below, using complete sentences and speaking Hejazi as naturally as you can.

dialogue.speaker: محلي
dialogue.transliteration: ahlan wa sahlan! ween tabi trooh?
dialogue.english: Welcome! Where do you want to go?

dialogue.speaker: سَائِح
dialogue.arabic: لَوْ سَمَحْتَ، أَبِي أَرُوح السُّوق. هَالْمَنْطَقَة جَدِيدَة عَلَى.
dialogue.transliteration: law samaht, abi arooh as-sooq. hal-mintaqa jadeeda 3alayya.
dialogue.english: Please, I want to go to the market. This area is new to me.

dialogue.speaker: محلي
dialogue.arabic: دُغْرِي مِنْ هِيهِ يَا أَخِي. لِفّ يَمِين عِنْدَ الإِشَارَة. السُّوق بِشَارِعِ الْمَلِكْ.
dialogue.transliteration: dughri min hiih ya akh. liff yameen 3ind al-ishara. as-sooq bi-shaari3 al-malik.
dialogue.english: Straight ahead my friend. Turn right at the traffic light. The market is on King Street.

dialogue.speaker: سَائِح
dialogue.english: Is it far?

dialogue.speaker: محلي
dialogue.arabic: لاَ، حَوَالَي عِشْرْ دَقَايِق عَلَى الرِّجْلَيْن.
dialogue.english: No, about ten minutes on foot.

dialogue.speaker: سَائِح
dialogue.english: Okay, thanks a lot for your help.

dialogue.speaker: محلي
dialogue.arabic: أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا. اِسْتَمْتِع بِالسُّوق يَا غَالِي!
dialogue.transliteration: ahlan wa sahlan. istamti3 bi-as-sooq ya ghali!
dialogue.english: You're welcome my friend! Enjoy the market!
